body.hook: Painters often keep a limited palette of only a few tubes of paint, yet they create hundreds of colours. The secret is knowing how colours mix. Today you'll mix a whole colour wheel from just three.

study.title: Mix the Wheel
study.question: How can three colours make a whole colour wheel?
study.passage:
Studio steps (written for this lesson):
1. Draw a 12-section colour wheel.
2. Paint the primaries in sections 1, 5 and 9: red, yellow, blue.
3. Mix and paint the secondaries halfway between: red + yellow = orange; yellow + blue = green; blue + red = violet.
4. Mix the six tertiaries: red-orange, yellow-orange, yellow-green, blue-green, blue-violet, red-violet. Tip: when mixing with yellow, add the darker colour to the yellow a tiny bit at a time.
5. Tints and shades strip: choose one colour. Paint it pure in the middle box, add a little white for each box to the right (tints) and a little black for each box to the left (shades).
6. Clean your brush between colours, and keep a paper towel handy.

body.hook: Why do fast-food logos use so much red and yellow, while banks and hospitals use blue? Colours carry temperatures and feelings. Warm colours seem to jump forward; cool colours seem to step back and calm us down.

vocabulary.definition: Reds, oranges and yellows; they feel energetic and seem to come forward.

study.title: Hot and Cold
study.question: How do warm and cool colours change the feeling and depth of an artwork?
study.passage:
Studio steps (written for this lesson):
1. Sort it: Sort 20 paint-chip colours into warm and cool. Some are tricky (a cool red, a warm green). Discuss why.
2. Complementary pairs: Find the three main pairs on your colour wheel: red and green, blue and orange, yellow and violet. Paint a small shape in one colour on a background of its complement. What happens at the edge?
3. Two moods: Draw the same simple landscape twice (hills, a tree, a sky). Paint one using only warm colours and one using only cool colours.
4. Depth: Paint a third version where the near hills are warm and strong and the far hills are cool, pale and less detailed. Compare the three.

body.objective: Students will be able to arrange a balanced composition.
body.iCan: I can arrange a balanced composition.
successCriteria: I can create symmetrical and asymmetrical balance
I can use pattern and repetition
I can plan a balanced composition using thumbnails
body.hook: Look at a page of a great comic or a famous photo. Your eye moves exactly where the artist wants it to. That isn't luck; it's composition: the way shapes, colours and spaces are arranged.

vocabulary.definition: The arrangement of the parts of an artwork.
How visual weight is spread so an artwork feels stable.
Both sides of an artwork are the same or very similar.
Different things on each side that still feel equal in weight.
Parts arranged around a centre, like a flower or a wheel.
A repeated design of shapes, lines or colours.

study.title: Arrange It
study.question: How does arrangement make an artwork feel balanced and interesting?
study.passage:
Studio steps (written for this lesson):
1. Balance sorting: Look at six images (a butterfly, a mandala, a photo of a lone tree off-centre, a cathedral front, a sunflower, a landscape with one big rock on the left and three small rocks on the right). Sort them into symmetrical, asymmetrical and radial balance.
2. Paper experiment: Using cut paper shapes (one big, three small, in two colours), arrange them on a background three ways: symmetrical, asymmetrical and radial. Photograph each.
3. Thumbnails: Draw four small thumbnails for a final artwork based on a natural theme (leaves, shells, insects, flowers). Try each type of balance and include a repeating pattern.
4. Final composition: Choose your best thumbnail and create it in coloured pencil or paint, using colours from your colour wheel and at least one pattern.
